A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

NL1 deletion results in an increase in indirect pathway MSNs and a decrease in N-methyl-Daspartate receptor-mediated currents in direct pathway MSNs, both of which could contribute to increased repetitive grooming behavior in NL1 KO animals.

NL1 deletion in the striatum leads to reduced NMDAR mediated synaptic currents in direct pathway MSNs, which is likely due to a reduction of GluN2 subunit expression and/or function, resulting in a decrease in the NMDA/AMPAR ratio and a decrease in repetitive grooming.

NL1 deletion in the mouse brain leads to a decrease in N-methyl-Daspartate receptor (NR1/GluN2A) mediated currents in medium spiny neurons of the direct pathway in the dorsal striatum, which may contribute to repetitive grooming behaviors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NL1 modulates striatum function in a pathway and receptor subunit specific manner.
NL1 deletion has distinct effects in the direct and in the indirect pathway of the striatum.
NL1 is a modulator of glutamatergicsynaptic transmission in a pathway-specific manner.
